title: Linked Structure
body:
Any collection where the elements are held together by [[Pointer]]s instead of by being
next to each other in [[Memory]]. The contrast with an [[Array]] is the point of the topic:

| | [[Array]] | Linked structure |
|---|---|---|
| Elements are | contiguous | scattered on the heap |
| Found by | arithmetic on the [[Index]] | following pointers from the front |
| Size | fixed at compile time | grows one [[Node]] at a time |
| Reach element *i* | instantly | walk *i* nodes |
| Insert in the middle | shuffle everything after it | reassign two pointers |
| Overhead | none | a pointer per node |

Neither wins. An array is fast to read and expensive to change; a linked structure is the
other way around. Which one to pick is a question this course cannot answer yet, and
[[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] answers with [[Time Complexity]].

The mechanism is always the same. Each node holds its data and the address of the next one,
allocated with [[new And delete|new]] when it is needed and reached from a single pointer to
the front:

```c++
Node* head = NULL;          // empty
head = new Node;            // one node
head->data = 7;
head->next = NULL;
```

Walking one is the loop you will write a hundred times:

```c++
Node* cur = head;
while (cur != NULL) {
	cout << cur->data << " ";
	cur = cur->next;
}
```

Use a *separate* pointer to walk. Advancing `head` itself loses the list.

The family: [[Linked List]] (one pointer per node), [[Singleton List]] (a list of one),
[[Tree]] (two), [[Graph]] (many). [[Stack]] and [[Queue]] are usually built out of one.
